question: Does a next-trade-sign model trained in 2023 go stale by 2026, and is the loss covariate shift or concept shift?

verdict.text: One month on (2023-06 model scored on 2023-07), the staleness gap of gbm_all is +0.19 pp [+0.06, +0.26] of accuracy (median of 10 symbols, 95% day-block interval), which is positive. This is the ordinary one-month drift yardstick. Yes. By 2026-07 the 2023-06 model is stale, and its staleness gap is larger than the one-month yardstick: G = +1.63 pp [+1.42, +1.85] against +0.19 pp, a difference of +1.03 pp [+0.83, +1.29] (8.5 times the yardstick). The gap is above the yardstick on 10 of 10 symbols and its own interval excludes zero from above on 10 of 10. Separately from staleness, the market itself became more predictable for a freshly trained model: D = +2.23 pp [+1.36, +3.21]. The raw drop of the old model, -0.08 pp, is G minus D, so retraining would recover +1.63 pp of it. Measured against each period's own one-lag baseline, fresh-model skill changed by +0.89 pp [-0.56, +1.74]. In log loss the staleness gap is +0.0217 bits [+0.0182, +0.0230]. Attribution of the 2023-06 model's log loss change to 2026-07 (-0.0059 bits; negative means the old model's loss fell): covariate part -0.0090 bits [-0.0101, -0.0045], concept residual -0.0000 bits [-0.0068, +0.0087]. No side dominates: by the cross-symbol median the larger side is the covariate part (the inputs moved), but the concept residual is the larger one on 6 of 10 symbols. Effective sample size is above the 10% threshold on 10 of 10 symbols (median share 37%). The weights are healthy on most symbols.
